response:
Curl-like B-mode patterns in the polarization of the cosmic microwave background are prized because, at degree angular scales, scalar density perturbations do not generate them directly, whereas a background of tensor perturbations, gravitational waves stretching spacetime during inflation, does. Other processes, however, imprint B-modes as well, and separating them requires measurements at more than one frequency, since each source scales differently with frequency. The BICEP2 collaboration announced its detection of B-mode polarization on March 17, 2014, and the debate that followed became a standard example of how a single-frequency measurement can be reassessed by multi-frequency data.

The BICEP2 telescope was located in Chile's Atacama Desert. BICEP2 reported a tensor-to-scalar ratio of r = 0.20. The collaboration took that amplitude to indicate a substantial tensor contribution, and the BICEP2 team interpreted the signal as evidence of primordial gravitational waves from cosmic inflation. Because BICEP2 observed only at 150 GHz, it could not measure foregrounds in its own field. It instead relied on dust models extrapolated from earlier, less sensitive data. Despite that inflationary reading, the Planck collaboration released dust polarization measurements at 353 GHz in September 2014, and the Planck 353 GHz data indicated that dust in the BICEP2 field was brighter than BICEP2 had assumed. The BICEP2, Keck Array, and Planck teams performed a joint cross-correlation analysis of their data.

The joint analysis confirmed a gravitational-wave detection at more than five sigma significance. Its method was to cross-correlate the 150 GHz maps from BICEP2 and Keck with Planck's higher-frequency maps, in which dust dominates. This allowed the spectral dependence of each component to be fitted rather than assumed. The brighter dust measured by Planck is direct evidence for the first of two non-primordial contributions, at least one of which, perhaps both, shaped the measurement: polarized Galactic dust emission contributed B-mode power in the BICEP2 observing field, or gravitational lensing of E-mode polarization contributed B-mode power there. Lensing arises when the gravitational potentials of intervening large-scale structure deflect CMB photons. This deflection converts a fraction of the E-mode pattern into B-modes, and theory predicts the size of that contribution once the E-mode spectrum is known.

With these components modeled, the interpretive question reduced to a strict dichotomy. Either the BICEP2 B-mode signal was produced primarily by primordial gravitational waves, or, in contrast to that five-sigma confirmation, the BICEP2 B-mode signal was not produced primarily by primordial gravitational waves. The two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. Deciding between them depended on whether any B-mode power remained after the dust template, scaled from 353 GHz to 150 GHz, and the predicted lensing spectrum were subtracted. A genuine tensor signal would appear as a residual excess at degree scales with the frequency dependence of the CMB itself. A dust-dominated signal would instead track the steeply rising spectrum that Planck observed at high frequency. Applying this test, the joint BICEP2/Keck/Planck team determined that the BICEP2 B-mode signal was not produced primarily by primordial gravitational waves.

The joint analysis set an upper limit on the tensor-to-scalar ratio of r < 0.12 at 95% confidence; in other words, it excluded tensor-to-scalar ratios of 0.12 or higher at 95% confidence. The originally reported value of r = 0.20 therefore fell outside the permitted range. The signal's non-primordial character indicates the decisive outcome, which settles the tension between the original inflationary interpretation and the Planck dust measurements. The joint BICEP2/Keck/Planck analysis concluded that no statistically significant evidence for primordial gravitational waves remained once dust was accounted for. The episode shaped the design of later experiments, which now observe at several frequencies precisely so that dust can be characterized within the observing field itself rather than inferred from external models.
